30.t: Duke's claim about writing 'Mood Indigo' at breakfast
30.s: Bigard laughs at Duke's article saying he wrote 'Mood Indigo' in fifteen minutes while his mother made breakfast, when Bigard says he gave Duke the last half and Duke added the first.
30.q: Yeah, at the last second. I mean, he was funny like that. I don't know why -- what caused him to do those kind of things. And another thing he did -- I had to laugh when I read that article -- he said he wrote "Mood Indigo" at his

30.t: Duke Ellington taking credit: Sophisticated Lady
30.s: Lawrence Brown and Otto Hardwick fooled with the tune in a dressing room and Duke turned it into 'Sophisticated Lady'; Bigard says Duke did not credit his men though he did compose good numbers.
30.q: Yeah, and I had to play the bridge in that (humming). Sure. Just like Lawrence Brown and Otto Hardwick, they made Sophisticated Lady.

921.t: The Tio family and Sophisticated Lady
921.s: Her father knew all the Tios; a man on London Avenue told her his brother Lorenzo wrote Sophisticated Lady and Mood Indigo, and Russell recalls Bigard saying the same.
921.q: So you could have known them. All the Tio's. There's one that lived right here on London Avenue. That's the one I was telling you about this morning, about the Duke of Ongton. Yeah. Oh yeah.

185.t: Lorenzo's tunes sold to Ellington and Bechet's debt to the family
185.s: Tio says Lorenzo wrote Sophisticated Lady and Mood Indigo material, Harlem Hot Shot with Steve Lewis, and that Sidney Bechet drew on his uncle and father.
185.ch: Brother Lorenzo Tio Jr. and his career
185.q: Mood Indigo was right. Well, that's what he made, he sold, a sophisticated lady was originally written by Lorenzo Keough, and that was written right here on Havana Street at 2404. That was before he went to New York. Then he had Mood Indigo and Mood Glow, and him and Steve Lewis, which I would like…

400.t: Duke Ellington taking credit: Cottontail and the IBM comparison
400.s: Hinton and Taylor discuss how Duke put his name on tunes like Ben Webster's Cottontail, how Tyree Glenn's piece changed, and whether it was fair.
400.ch: Armstrong, Ellington, Ben Webster, family loss and mentoring
400.q: I know one time we were going someplace and the two bands were going the same place. The trains hooked our two cars together, from Chicago to Omaha. What a great time we had, you know with the two cars together, the two bands sitting around drinking and talking and riding the train. And Ben had…

145.s: Royal doubts who wrote what, noting Irving Mills's name is on much of Duke's work.
145.ch: Les Hite, Sebastian's and Duke Ellington
145.q: I haven't got the slightest idea. Nope. That was all inside stuff, the writing and a whole lot of things, a whole lot of people have been given credit for the writing of things, down through the years, that had nothing absolutely to do with the writing.

409.t: Other Ellington compositions and Billy Strayhorn writing for Johnny Hodges
409.s: Who wrote on Sophisticated Lady and other numbers; Strayhorn wrote for Johnny Hodges when Cootie was there.
409.q: Yeah. It was an instrumental. The first record that came out on "Do Nothing Till You Hear From Me", was "Concerto for Cootie".

380.t: Who wrote "Night Train" and "Happy Go Lucky Local"
380.s: Callender and Willard agree Ellington wrote it, that Jimmy Forrest took the credit, and that Ellington never sued, unlike Tizol over "Patricia".
380.ch: Los Angeles, Ellington and the recording scene
380.q: Oh, it was probably ten or twelve years before "Night Train." Oh, it was an open secret. Everybody knew Duke wrote it. But Jimmy Forrest recorded it and put his name on it, and... Well, he got the credit for "Night Train." But everybody knows that it was "Happy Go Lucky Local" that knew anything…

6.t: Did Duke take too much credit? Irving Mills and the hustler
6.s: Procope agrees Duke was a hustler who borrowed ideas from band members, possibly getting back at Irving Mills, whose name was on every bar of Duke's early music.
6.q: That's true, and what -- yeah, I can move over here. That's true, because you see, Duke Ellington was a man -- Duke Ellington was what we used to call in the old days a hustler. Duke liked to say he was raised in a pool room, which he wasn't actually, but that gave you an inkling as to his…

237.s: Smith raises the Bigard claim; Goodwin says there was little doubt locally that Ellington wrote it but no proof either way.

76.t: Papa Tio and the origin of Mood Indigo
76.s: Zutty and Marge say Tio taught many clarinetists and that Mood Indigo came from him through Barney Bigard to Duke Ellington. They puzzle over the credits on records, including Mills.
76.q: Yes. You see, because I met Tio's daughter out in a country town here in New York State, and she was still kind of salty with Barney Bigard because he let Duke have this thing of, he let Duke have this thing, 'Mood Indigo' because they claim, Barney told me that Duke put more, a little more…

77.t: Porter Granger, the gentleman who tried to polish Bessie
77.s: Granger worked with Hunter, wrote "Michigan Water Tastes Like Sherry Wine", wrote whole shows and never got credit.
77.q: Good. Well, I made that with him. And so many things that he didn't get credit for.
